Endless
ěnd´lěs
adj. (without end; used of Christ's life and priesthood, and of the genealogies that go nowhere)
From end + -less. The KJV uses it for two different Greek words: akatalutos, indissoluble, of Christ's life; and aperantos, without limit, of the fables Timothy is to refuse. The same English word covers a glory and a futility.

Biblical Definition

Hebrews grounds the superiority of Christ's priesthood in the kind of life He has: “Who is made, not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life” (Hebrews 7:16). The Greek is akatalutos — not merely long, but indissoluble, incapable of being broken up. Aaron's sons died and were replaced; this Priest cannot be. The consequence follows at once: “But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood” (Hebrews 7:24), and then the pastoral conclusion the whole argument exists for: “Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). A believer's security rests on the fact that his Advocate does not have a term of office. The same English word carries the opposite weight elsewhere: “Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do” (1 Timothy 1:4). There is an endlessness that is life and an endlessness that is only a corridor — a study that never arrives, questions that breed questions, and no edifying at the end of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines endless as without end; having no end or conclusion; perpetual; interminable; and also, incessant, continual.

expand to see more

ENDLESS, a. Without end; having no end or conclusion; applied to length, and to duration; as an endless line; endless progression; endless duration; endless bliss.

ENDLESS, a. Perpetual; incessant; continual; as endless praise; endless clamor.

ENDLESSLY, adv. Without end or termination; incessantly; perpetually.

INDISSOLUBLE, a. [L. indissolubilis.] That cannot be dissolved, melted or liquefied; not to be broken or rightfully violated; perpetually binding.

GENEALOGY, n. [Gr.] An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor; enumeration of ancestors in order of succession.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 7:16 — "Who is made, not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life."

Hebrews 7:24 — "But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood."

Hebrews 7:25 — "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

1 Timothy 1:4 — "Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do."

Modern Corruption

Endlessness is taken as a bare quantity of time, so that an endless life is heard as a very long one and an endless punishment as an argument against God's love.

expand to see more

Hebrews 7:16 does not say Christ's life is lengthy; it says it is akatalutos, unable to be dissolved. The difference is the difference between a long lease and a freehold. This is why verse 25 can promise salvation to the uttermost: the intercession does not lapse because the Intercessor cannot lapse. A believer who conceives of eternal life as duration rather than as an indissoluble life shared with Christ has the arithmetic and not the security.

The same category error drives the modern rejection of eternal punishment. Annihilationism and universalism both argue that endless suffering is disproportionate, treating the sentence as a quantity of time set against a quantity of offence. Scripture uses one word, aionios, for the life of the redeemed and the punishment of the lost in a single verse, Matthew 25:46, and the 1689 confesses both. An argument that shortens the one has shortened the other, and the same reasoning that says God's love would not permit an unending punishment has quietly made God's love the judge of God's justice.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek akatalutos (G179), indissoluble; aperantos (G562), without limit; aparabatos (G531), unchangeable, untransferable; aionios (G166), eternal.

expand to see more

Greek akatalutos (G179) — that cannot be dissolved; Hebrews 7:16, the power of an endless life.

Greek aperantos (G562) — unlimited, interminable; 1 Timothy 1:4, the genealogies that go nowhere.

Greek aparabatos (G531) — not passing to a successor; Hebrews 7:24, the unchangeable priesthood.

Greek panteles (G3838) — to the uttermost, completely; Hebrews 7:25.

Greek aionios (G166) — eternal; Matthew 25:46, one word over both the life and the punishment.

Usage

"“The power of an endless life” — indissoluble, not merely long."

"“He ever liveth to make intercession” — the Advocate has no term of office."

"“Endless genealogies, which minister questions” — a study that never arrives."
